summary.text: A two-year-old boy was brought to an eye doctor with photophobia and had persistent pupillary membranes in both eyes. He was delivered as a breech baby at 39 weeks weighing 3100 g without complications. At age three years visual acuity was 0.4 in the right eye and 0.3 in the left eye, and a topical tropicamide and phenylephrine combination was started twice daily at that age.

At age five years visual acuity without glasses was 0.6 right and 0.7 left, and severe photophobia troubled him in daily life. At age six years he underwent resection of pupillary membranes in both eyes under general anesthesia. In the right eye vitreous cutter excision took time, so hyaluronate, scissors and forceps were used and the chamber was washed; the left eye was done with scissors and forceps from the start, shorter in time.

He did not complain of photophobia after the resection and showed visual acuity of 1.2 in both eyes without correction, with no amblyopia per the authors. He did not develop cataract, glaucoma or other surgical complications until the last follow-up at age 17 years, with clear cornea and clear lens at that visit.

Pathology of the excised membranes showed vascular lumen with red blood cells in both eyes. Immunostaining of the left-eye membrane showed vascular lumen-lining cells positive for CD31 and ERG and negative for D2-40, and most pigment-bearing cells positive for D2-40. Functional vision assessment tests were not performed.

summary.text: A one-month-old female baby, born at 37 weeks weighing 2668 g without complications in pregnancy, was brought to an eye doctor with persistent pupillary membranes in both eyes. The right cornea was clear at 9 mm and the left cornea showed temporal-half opacity at 6 mm, with an iris process inserted into the opacity, indicative of Peters' anomaly.

The left cornea became clear at six months, esotropia of the left eye was noted at one year, and full-correction glasses were begun at three years based on cycloplegic refraction. Topical 1% atropine was started at six months, with the starting frequency reported inconsistently, and was used once a week until the latest visit at 12 years; 0.5% timolol once daily and 1% brinzolamide twice daily were begun in the left eye at ten years.

At 12 years best-corrected visual acuity was 0.7 in the right eye and 0.06 in the left, and optical coherence tomography showed normal anterior chamber depth on the right and a shallow chamber with iris process adhesion to the inner corneal surface on the left. Intraocular pressure was 16 and 20 mmHg and stayed in the normal range with the drops. No surgery was done, and she had no vision problems in learning at school.

summary.text: A 49-year-old woman visited an eye doctor with decreased vision in both eyes. She had been told in childhood that she had persistent pupillary membranes in both eyes, and took escitalopram for anxiety and olmesartan and amlodipine for hypertension. Best-corrected visual acuity was 0.1 right and 0.2 left, with anterior and posterior subcapsular cataracts in both eyes and pterygium on the right.

Fundus examinations with mydriasis were normal. She did not wish to have surgery due to anxiety, so glasses for myopia were prescribed. At age 56 years she underwent cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation in the right and then the left eye, one week apart, with the pupillary membrane cut with scissors and pulled out with forceps in the hyaluronate-filled anterior chamber first.

Pathology of the excised tissue showed vascular structures with red blood cells in the lumen, with vascular lumen-lining cells positive for CD31 and ERG and negative for D2-40. At the last follow-up one year after surgery best-corrected visual acuity was 0.5 in both eyes, with clear pupillary areas and intraocular lenses in both eyes.

Surgical procedures to excise pupillary membranes (Case 1)Surgical procedures for resection of persistent pupillary membrane at the age of six years. In the right eye, with the time sequence from A, B, C, to D, a 25-gauge vitreous cutter was used under irrigation with a 25-gauge infusion cannula in the first phase (A). In the left eye with the time sequence from E, F, G, to H, scissors were used at the first place to cut the roots on the iris surface (arrows, E, F), the isolated membrane was pulled out with forceps (G), and the anterior chamber was washed finally with a vitreous cutter under the irrigation with an infusion cannula (H).

article_limitations: Caption-layer figure fields are not_inspected; actual figure pixels are reviewed in the visual submission.
Visual acuity is reported in decimals; correction details are kept as printed text and no unit or conversion is applied.

Case 2 starting atropine frequency differs between the case presentation (once every week or two weeks) and the discussion and Table 1 (once a week); only that attribute is quarantined as source_conflict.
Atropine side effects such as salivation are mentioned as the basis for the dosing interval, not as events in the patient, and are not recorded as adverse effects.
Authors hedge the interpretation of the CD31 and ERG fascicular pattern as probably a longitudinal section of vessels and possibly a melanin artifact.
Functional vision assessment tests are stated as not performed in the present series of patients; recorded for each of the three patients on that explicit series-wide statement.
Discussion sentence attributed to a case series by named authors explicitly names this child (Case 1) as free of cataract until adulthood; kept only as extra evidence on the no-cataract fact.
Case 3 cataract surgery is stated as performed ("performed as usual", Table 1, "underwent cataract surgeries"); the eye sequence and one-week interval come from the decision sentence.
The Case 3 case text cites Figure 5C for the surgical step, whereas the caption and pixels show hematoxylin-eosin histology of the excised membrane.
The Case 2 case text cites Figures 4C and 4D for drops begun at age 10 years while the caption dates those panels to age nine years.
